sections.label: Global investment screening frameworks
sections.summary: A 2023 UN report says at least 37 countries have introduced investment screening frameworks since the 1990s, with more countries recently acting.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: According to a 2023 United Nations report, at least 37 countries have introduced regulatory frameworks for the screening of investments on national security grounds since the 1990s.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: More recently, countries like Australia, China, Japan, Ireland, the United Kingdom (UK) and the United States (US) have introduced or enhanced their investment management regimes, with more planning to do so.

sections.label: Significant Investments Review Bill purpose
sections.summary: The Bill complements existing sectoral safeguards by introducing a new investment management regime.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: The Significant Investments Review Bill is designed to complement the existing suite of sectoral safeguards, by introducing a new investment management regime.

sections.label: Minister designating entities
sections.summary: Clause 17 allows the Minister to designate a specific entity based on national security considerations.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: Clause 17 allows the Minister to designate a specific entity based on national security considerations.

sections.label: Few designations expected in Singapore
sections.summary: Most entities in these sectors will be regulated, but Singapore expects to designate only a handful as most critical entities are already covered.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: Most entities within these sectors or performing such activities will be regulated.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: But for Singapore, as the majority of critical entities here are already covered by existing sectoral legislation, we expect to designate only a handful of entities.

sections.label: Controller notification and approval thresholds
sections.summary: Buyers must notify the Minister within seven days of becoming a 5% controller and seek approval before becoming a 12%, 25% or 50% controller.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: Buyers are required to notify the Minister within seven days after becoming a 5% controller.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: They will need to seek the Minister's approval before becoming a 12%, 25% or 50% controller.

sections.label: Void transactions without approval
sections.summary: Clause 21 automatically renders transactions void if controllers proceed without the necessary prior approvals from the Minister.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: Should prospective or existing controllers proceed with the transactions without seeking the necessary prior approvals from the Minister, clause 21 automatically renders such transactions void.

sections.label: Minister review of ownership transactions
sections.summary: Clause 32 lets the Minister review ownership or control transactions only if the entity acted against national security and the transaction occurred within two years prior.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: In Singapore's case, under clause 32, the Minister can review ownership or control transactions involving any entity only if two pre-requisites are met.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: First, the entity must have acted against our national security interests, and not merely pose potential threats to our national security.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: Second, the ownership or control transaction must have occurred within the two years prior to the above-mentioned action by the entity against our national security interests.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: The Minister for Home Affairs, as the Minister-in-charge of internal security, can issue a certificate stating that he is satisfied that the entity has acted against the national security interest of Singapore; which will be treated as conclusive evidence for the purposes of this Bill.

sections.label: Maximum penalty for individuals and entities
sections.summary: Maximum penalties are based on the higher of an absolute quantum cap or transaction value, or for entities without transaction value, 10% of annual turnover.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: As such, for both individuals and entities, the maximum applicable penalty will be based on the higher of an absolute quantum cap or the transaction value, where applicable.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: If there is no transaction value, for entities, the maximum penalty will be based on the higher of an absolute quantum cap or 10% of the annual turnover.

sections.label: Reconsideration and Reviewing Tribunal appeals
sections.summary: Clauses 38 and 39 set out processes for parties to seek reconsideration from the Minister and make further appeals to an independent Reviewing Tribunal.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: Clauses 38 and 39 set out processes for parties that wish to seek reconsideration from the Minister for his decisions and to make further appeals to an independent Reviewing Tribunal.

sections.label: Office of Significant Investments Review
sections.summary: The Office of Significant Investments Review will be set up under the Ministry of Trade and Industry.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: Under the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI), we will set up the Office of Significant Investments Review.

sections.label: Entities critical to economy and society
sections.summary: Such entities are critical to the economy and society, and may act detrimentally to national interest as owners or operators advance strategic or economic interests.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: Such entities are also critical to the proper functioning of our economy and society.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: We cannot rule out the possibility that, as the business owners or operators advance their strategic or economic interest, there could be potential situations where these entities may act in way that is detrimental to our national interest.

sections.label: New laws protecting strategic assets
sections.summary: Rising geopolitical tensions and concerns over national economic security and strategic competition have led more countries to introduce legislation protecting strategically important technologies, assets and key infrastructures.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: With rising geopolitical tensions and concerns over national economic security and strategic competition, we have seen more countries introduce new legislations to protect strategically important technologies, assets and key infrastructures, such as the CHIPS and Science Act in the US and the Export Control Law in China.

sections.label: Bill objective for critical entities
sections.summary: The Bill aims to ensure critical entities continue providing their functions securely and reliably over time.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: The objective this Bill is to ensure that the critical entities continue providing their functions securely and reliably over time.

sections.label: Two-year time bar question
sections.summary: A question asks the Minister for the consideration behind the two-year time bar for entities acting against national security interest.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: Thirdly, with regard to the two-year time bar for entities that have acted against our national security interest, can I ask the Minister on the consideration behind this parameter of two years?

sections.label: Designated entities under investment regime
sections.summary: Under the new investment management regime, entities critical to Singapore's national security interests will be identified as designated entities and regulated.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Under the new investment management regime, entities that are critical to Singapore's national security interests will be identified as "designated entities" and will be regulated, and these include entities which are not currently covered under existing legislation to monitor and manage entities in sectors, such as telecommunications, banking and utilities.

sections.label: Public list of designated entities
sections.summary: A Member says making public the list of designated entities will signal that most of the market is open for investment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: In the November 2023 press release by MTI, Minister Gan shared that, "we expect only a handful of critical entities to be designated under this Bill".

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: While I can understand if the Government does not wish to disclose the identities of non-designated entities but which it is otherwise monitoring for national security concerns, making public the list of designated entities will signal to businesses that the vast majority of the market is open for investment and that the scope of SIRA is truly limited to just a handful of companies.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: To be clear, I am not saying that SIRA is unnecessary because of existing control mechanisms, but on the contrary, I believe that the formalisation of SIRA will allow international businesses to have greater confidence in the regulatory environment in which investments into Singapore are made, with the scoping of provisions under SIRA providing greater regulatory certainty to businesses.

sections.label: Five percent notification threshold rationale
sections.summary: A question asks the rationale for the 5% threshold at which acquirers of designated entities must notify the Minister.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Thirdly, on notification thresholds, CFIUS requires the authorities to be notified if a foreign party obtains 25% or more voting interest in critical technologies, critical infrastructure and sensitive personal data (TID) businesses; and a foreign government, except for Australia, Canada, and the UK, holds a 49% or more voting interest in the foreign party.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: What is the rationale for the designation of 5% as the threshold in which acquirers of designated entities must notify the Minister?

sections.label: National security interests undefined
sections.summary: A Member observes that the phrase national security interests is not defined anywhere in the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The first thing I observed is that, even though the primary purpose of this Bill is to safeguard Singapore's national security interests, the phrase "national security interests" does not appear to be defined anywhere in the Bill.

sections.label: Minister appoints and removes key officers
sections.summary: Clauses 27 and 28 empower the Minister to decide on appointing and to remove key officers of designated entities.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Second, clause 27 empowers the Minister to decide on the appointment of key officers of designated entities, such as the chief executive officer, directors and chairpersons, and similarly, clause 28 empowers the Minister the remove such key officers.

sections.label: FICA, SIRA, courts and transparency
sections.summary: Speaker contrasts FICA and SIRA, asks why courts are excluded, and urges justifiable, transparent implementation with regular public accounting.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: While FICA deals with counteracting acts of foreign interference and specifically aimed at politically significant persons, where the evidence rely heavily on sensitive intelligence and collaboration with foreign counterparts; SIRA deals with investment decisions made by businesses where, yes, there can be the possibility of insidious parties masquerading as legitimate businesses, but where I would imagine the threat to our national security interests depend more on the nature of the industry sector, that type of goods and services provided to Singaporeans and the business activities that are carried out here.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: What is the rationale for disallowing the role of the courts, particularly when our reputation as an international business hub relies heavily on upholding the rule of law itself?

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: To conclude, Mr Speaker, I recognise the importance of safeguarding critical entities and infrastructure in Singapore and in taking preventive and corrective actions to protect our national security interests.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: It is also as important that we ensure the implementation of the Act and the exercise of powers conferred are done in a justifiable and transparent manner, with decisions made publicly accounted for on a regular basis, such as in other jurisdictions, where practicable.

sections.label: National security and economic interest balance
sections.summary: Speaker asks how the Bill balances national security and economic interest without harming Singapore's competitive business environment and trade obligations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
sentences.text: Can the Minister clarify, how the Bill will balance national security and economic interest without adversely impacting Singapore's competitive business environment?

sentences.speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
sentences.text: How does this Bill comply with Singapore's existing trade obligations?

sections.label: Significant investments and critical entity criteria
sections.summary: Speaker asks for a more comprehensive definition of significant investments and the criteria for designating entities as critical for national security.

sentences.speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
sentences.text: Would the Minister provide a more comprehensive definition of what constitutes as "significant investments" under this Bill?

sentences.speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
sentences.text: What criteria will the Minister use to designate entities as critical for national security?

sections.label: Screening regime for ownership transactions
sections.summary: The proposed Bill sets up a screening regime for ownership transactions in critical business entities.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Under the proposed Bill, a screening regime for ownership transactions in critical business entities will be set up.

sections.label: Supporting Bill without knowing affected areas
sections.summary: Speaker states Parliament is asked to support the Bill without knowing which economic areas and companies are likely to be affected.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Today, Parliament is asked to support the Bill without knowing which are the economic areas and companies that are likely to be affected.

sections.label: Tribunal decisions final, judicial review ouster
sections.summary: Section 46 makes the Reviewing Tribunal's decision final and not challengeable in any other Court.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Fourthly, while the decisions by a Minister would still be appealable to an independent Reviewing Tribunal, section 46 of the proposed Bill is a judicial review ouster clause, which provides that the Tribunal's decision is final and cannot be challenged, appealed against, reviewed, quashed or called into action in any other Court of law.

sections.label: PSP opposes Bill without amendments
sections.summary: PSP opposes the Bill unless the provisions discussed above are amended.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Without amendments to the provisions discussed above, PSP opposes this Bill.

sections.label: PSP does not support Bill
sections.summary: PSP says focus should be on resilience of entities without the Singaporean Core, and does not support the Bill in its current form.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Rather, we should focus on the resilience of such entities where the Singaporean Core is no longer overseeing and manning them.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: PSP does not support this Bill in its current form.

sections.label: National security interest undefined in Bill
sections.summary: The Bill uses the term national security interest extensively but does not define it, and the term is unique to this Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The term "national security interest" is used extensively in the Bill but is not defined in the Bill; and the term "national security interest", in that order – "national", "security", "interest" – also appears to be quite unique to this Bill.

sections.label: Clarification sought on national security interest
sections.summary: The speaker seeks clarification from the Minister on the definition of national security interest and whether it aligns with Minister Yaacob Ibrahim's definition of considerations of national interest.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In this regard, I would like to seek clarification from the Minister as to the definition of "national security interest" in the Bill; and specifically, whether it would be aligned with the definition of "considerations of national interest" as elaborated by Minister Yaacob Ibrahim in the context of the Films (Amendment) Bill, which I mentioned earlier, or otherwise.

sections.label: Share price effects and Bill's importance
sections.summary: The speaker asks how the Government will ameliorate adverse share price effects on designated entities, and says the Bill is an important chink in Singapore's armour.

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In such an event, how will the Government ameliorate any adverse effect on the share price of such companies if they are announced to be on the list of designated entities, so as to avoid undue effects on investors, in particular, retail investors, in these companies?

sentences.speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The above having been said, this Bill is an important chink in our armour against undue influence that may be used against Singapore's interests and will complement existing legislation to protect Singapore's national security and economy.

sections.label: Similar legislation in other countries
sections.summary: Similar legislation has been passed in many countries, including some OECD countries and China, with more nations expected to follow.

sentences.speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Similar legislation had been passed in many countries in recent years, including a few Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries and China.

sentences.speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: More nations are expected to follow, as governments scrutinise inward foreign direct investments (FDIs) ever more rigorously to enhance economic resilience and national security.

sentences.speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: The new Bill could plug the policy loopholes created by today's international strategic investment environment.

sections.label: Concern about FDI impact
sections.summary: The speaker is concerned about the Bill's potential dampening impact on Singapore's foreign direct investment.

sentences.speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: While I am glad to note that the Bill was crafted in consultation with industry representatives to take into account the potential impact on businesses and investors, I am concerned about the potential dampening impact on our FDI.

sections.label: EU member states measures
sections.summary: As of April 2023, 24 of 27 EU member states have introduced or are introducing similar measures.

sentences.speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: For example, as of April 2023, 24 out of the 27 member states of the European Union have already introduced or are in the process of introducing similar measures.

sections.label: Transaction limit and undesignation process
sections.summary: The speaker suggests a S$400 million minimum transaction value and asks about the process for designated entities to be undesignated.

sentences.speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: To maintain the transparency, consistency and clarity that investors desire, perhaps a high-dollar limit for a minimum transaction value of S$400 million be established for such foreign investments to be included in this process.

sentences.speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In my view, in the current geopolitical environment, such a broader proposal for a more comprehensive Bill would be understood and readily accepted by foreign investors.

sentences.speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Also, many large institutional investors cannot invest in designated entities unless there is a clear mechanism for those designated entities to potentially regain their undesignated status.

sentences.speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Can the Minister perhaps share information on the process that is being established for such designated entities to be undesignated in the future?

sections.label: Office of Significant Investments Review framework
sections.summary: The Bill establishes the Office of Significant Investments Review and a framework to regulate significant investments in entities crucial to Singapore's national security.

sentences.speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The establishment of the Office of Significant Investments Review also provides a very useful dedicated one-stop touchpoint for all stakeholders.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: This Bill sets out a framework to regulate significant investments, whether originating locally or internationally, in entities deemed crucial to the national security interests of Singapore.

sections.label: Risk assessment tool proposal
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether the Ministry will consider developing an evidence-based risk assessment tool for all Ministries to identify national security issues.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In light of the above, will the Ministry consider developing an evidence-based robust and flexible risk assessment tool that can be used across all Ministries to identify what is and what is not an issue of national security?

sections.label: Australia investment screening guidelines
sections.summary: Australia uses publicly available sectoral guidance and national interests and national security tests in investment screening, and the speaker supports establishing such an office.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Similar guidelines are currently in use in Australia, where they have established publicly available sectoral guidance.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: They have also implemented national interests and national security tests as part of their investment screening policy.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I support the establishment of such an office and ask the Minister whether the office is to be established under the current Bill with its roles and function defined by legislation.

sections.label: Support for the Bill
sections.summary: The speaker quotes a remark that Singapore must have something special and be relied upon, and supports the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: On that occasion, he noted, "We must always have that something special that convinces the world that we are better bad than most and that Singapore can always be relied upon to deliver." Mr Speaker, clarifications notwithstanding, I support the Bill.

sections.label: Differing notice requirements
sections.summary: Section 18(5) requires the accused to notify the Minister within seven days, while section 19(12)(c) requires only all reasonable steps to notify within seven days.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Section 18(5) requires the accused to notify the Minister within seven days of contravening a notice requirement.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Section 19(12)(c) only requires the accused to take "all reasonable steps" to notify the Minister within seven days of contravening a separate notice requirement.

sections.label: Unwinding transactions within two years
sections.summary: The broad powers in this part of the Bill mean such transactions may be unwound within two years after they are concluded.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The broad powers in this part of the Bill mean that such transactions may be unwound within two years after they are concluded.

sections.label: Reviewing Tribunal and judicial review
sections.summary: Because judicial review is limited by section 46, the Reviewing Tribunal substantively performs the Supreme Court's function in reviewing the Minister's powers under the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: As the scope of judicial review is limited by section 46, the Reviewing Tribunal substantively performs the function of the Supreme Court in reviewing the Minister's powers under this Bill.

sections.label: Office of Significant Investments Review
sections.summary: The speaker calls the dedicated Office of Significant Investments Review a positive one-stop touchpoint and is glad the Bill's rules will not retroactively apply.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In addition, the establishment of a dedicated Office of Significant Investments Review as a one-stop touchpoint is a positive move and will help to ensure that key issues and concerns are addressed expediently.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I am glad that the Minister has made clear that the rules of this proposed Bill will not retroactively apply.

sections.label: Minister review notice period
sections.summary: Under section 32(3), a Minister may publish review notices within two years after a transaction, and may later order directions under section 32(5).

sentences.speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Under section 32(3), a Minister is allowed to publish notices to review transactions within a period of two years after any transaction.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: After such notice, the Minister may at any time thereafter order directions under section 32(5).

sentences.speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: This means that businesses may be subjected to potential scrutiny and uncertainty for an indefinite, undefined time period even after transactions are completed.

sections.label: No appeals against Special Administration Orders
sections.summary: The Act currently has no provision allowing appeals against Special Administration Orders, which may change a designated entity's management, business and property.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: For instance, there is currently no provision within the Act that allows for appeals against Special Administration Orders, even though such orders may potentially result in significant changes in the management of the affairs, business and property of a designated entity.

sections.label: Bill's economic growth impact
sections.summary: The speaker acknowledges safeguarding national security but says the Bill's potential impact on economic growth, transparency and accountability must be thoroughly considered.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: While acknowledging the imperative of safeguarding our national security, I believe in the critical need to thoroughly consider this Bill's potential impact on our economic growth, transparency and accountability.

sections.label: Vague national security interests guidelines
sections.summary: The vague delineation of national security interests requires clear guidelines and a robust oversight mechanism.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: The vague delineation of "national security interests" necessitates clear guidelines and a robust oversight mechanism.

sections.label: UK investigated French acquisition
sections.summary: In 2023, the UK government investigated the proposed acquisition of two UK businesses by a wholly-owned UK subsidiary of a French state-owned company.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: For instance, in 2023, the UK government investigated the proposed acquisition of two UK businesses by a wholly-owned UK subsidiary of a French state-owned company.

sections.label: Manpower for Office of Significant Investments Review
sections.summary: Sufficient manpower and resources are needed, and the Minister earlier mentioned an Office of Significant Investments Review will be set up.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: We need to ensure that there is sufficient manpower and resources to facilitate this.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: I note that the Minister earlier mentioned that an Office of Significant Investments Review will be set up.

sections.label: Openness to investments and security risk
sections.summary: The Bill is introduced to safeguard Singapore's national security interests, as its open investment environment leaves it vulnerable to malicious actors.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: In recent decades, countries have increasingly embraced openness to investments, fostering economic growth through joint ventures, local partnerships and mergers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: However, with these investments comes the risk of malicious actors exerting undue influence over entities, compromising a nation's security interests.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: In Singapore's context, with an open investment environment, we remain vulnerable to the risk of malicious actors seeking to gain control of our critical entities.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: It is therefore imperative that we introduce this Bill to safeguard our national security interests.

sections.label: Clarifications on the Bill's impact
sections.summary: The speaker lists six earlier clarifications, covering foreign investment impact, guidelines, economic balance, minority shareholders, review process and resources.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: In closing, I draw your attention to the earlier clarifications, namely: (a) the potential impact on foreign investment due to the Bill's broad definition of "national security interests"; (b) the necessity for clear guidelines and robust oversight mechanisms to ensure transparency and accountability in applying the Bill; (c) the delicate balance between national security and economic growth, and the risk of overly-stringent regulations hindering our long-term economic objectives; (d) the importance of safeguarding the rights and interests of minority shareholders within designated entities; (e) the imperative for a streamlined, efficient, and transparent review process that fosters trust and confidence in investors; and (f) the question of the adequate resources for the new Office of Significant Investments Review and the potential implications for national security considerations.

sections.label: Australia rejected SGX-ASX takeover
sections.summary: In 2011, the Australian Treasurer rejected the Singapore Stock Exchange's takeover of ASX Limited, ruling it could undermine Australia's financial centre position.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: If Members of this House remember in 2011, the Australian Treasurer rejected the takeover of ASX Limited by the Singapore Stock Exchange, ruling that the takeover could undermine Australia's position as a financial centre as well as jeopardise the stability of the country's financial system.

sections.label: Unclear criteria for national security interests
sections.summary: The Bill regulates significant investments to protect national security interests, but the specific criteria for national security interests are unclear.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: Second, the Bill seeks to protect the "national security interests" of Singapore by regulating significant investments in, and control of, critical entities.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: But like many speakers in this House, it is unclear what specific criteria, in regard to "national security interests", apply to entities under the Significant Investments Review Bill.

sections.label: Request for guidance on sensitive areas
sections.summary: The speaker asks the Minister to state generally the sensitive areas the Bill may cover, such as critical infrastructure, advanced technologies, data and defence.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: However, investors will need a clearer set of definitions and guidance to understand how entities are designated and classified in practice.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: So, I would like to ask the Minister whether the Government can provide further insights by stating, generally, sensitive areas that may be covered by the Bill such as critical infrastructure, advanced technologies, data and personal information, military and defence, public services and utilities or critical supply chain components.

sections.label: CFIUS timeline and Reviewing Tribunal
sections.summary: CFIUS commits to a 45-day review period, while the Bill provides for a Reviewing Tribunal chaired by a Supreme Court judge.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: For example, the CFIUS commits to a specific timeline for its review process, such as a 45-day review period, once a filing is accepted as complete.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: Currently, the Bill has provision for the setting up of a Reviewing Tribunal with members appointed by the President, at the advisement of the Cabinet, and the chairperson must be a Supreme Court judge.

sections.label: Number of critical entities
sections.summary: The Minister is asked how many critical entities the new regime will capture at the start and how the list may grow or change.

sentences.speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
sentences.text: Could the Minister clarify how many critical entities are expected to be captured under this new regime at the start and how the list may grow or change over time?

sections.label: Significant investments under Bill
sections.summary: The focus is on entities significant to Singapore's national security interests, rather than a more expansive approach used by other overseas investment screening regimes.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: Mr Shawn Huang asked what constitutes "significant investments" under this Bill.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: We will focus on entities that would be significant to Singapore's national security interests, rather than to take a more expansive and comprehensive approach that other overseas investment screening regimes have adopted, as suggested by Mr Neil Parekh.

sections.label: Defining national security threats
sections.summary: Providing a specific definition of national security or examples of threats would constrain quick action on new risks and expose Singapore's vulnerabilities.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: Providing a specific definition of "national security" or specific examples of such threats would not only constrain our ability to act quickly to address new risks that may emerge over time, but also expose Singapore's vulnerabilities.

sections.label: Bill and sectoral legislation
sections.summary: The Bill is not omnibus legislation and does not supersede ownership and control provisions in sectoral legislation.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: The Bill is not an omnibus legislation and does not supersede ownership and control provisions in sectoral legislation.

sections.label: Consultation with designated entities
sections.summary: All entities considered for designation have been reached out to and are in close discussions to understand their perspectives and mitigate regulatory impact.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: As mentioned in my Second Reading speech, we have reached out to all the entities that are being considered for designation and are in close discussions with them to understand their perspectives and explore ways to mitigate the regulatory impact on them.

sections.label: Future expansion of entity list
sections.summary: The list of entities is not expected to significantly expand soon, and additions will be carefully considered based on necessity for Singapore's national security.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: Nonetheless, we do not expect to significantly expand the list of entities in the near future.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: The addition of any entity to the list will be a carefully considered decision, which will continue to be based on whether designation is necessary in the interests of Singapore's national security.

sections.label: Conditions for exercising Bill powers
sections.summary: Two conditions must be met before powers under the Bill can be exercised: the entity acted against national security interests, and the transaction occurred within two years prior.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: As mentioned in my Second Reading speech, two conditions must be met before powers under the Bill can be exercised.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: First, the entity must have acted against our national security interests and not merely pose potential threats to our national security.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: Second, the ownership or control transaction must have occurred within the two years prior to the above-mentioned action by the entity against our national security interests.

sections.label: Reviewing Tribunal information reliance
sections.summary: The Reviewing Tribunal will be able to rely on all available information in making its decision on the appeal.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: As such, the Reviewing Tribunal will be able to rely on all available information in making its decision on the appeal.

sections.label: Courts unsuitable as oversight body
sections.summary: Ill-intentioned parties may threaten national security via ownership and control transactions, and Courts are unsuitable as oversight given sensitive intelligence evidence.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: As Mr Chua himself has pointed out, there is the possibility of ill-intentioned parties threatening our national security interests via ownership and control transactions.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: It will not be suitable to make the Courts serve as an oversight body, given that decisions under the Bill may involve national security considerations and may, indeed, rely on evidence from intelligence sources that would be highly sensitive.

sections.label: Office of Significant Investments Review
sections.summary: The Office of Significant Investments Review will be set up under MTI as the Competent Authority to administer and operationalise the Act.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum had some queries about the implementation of the Act.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
sentences.text: We will set up the Office of Significant Investments Review under MTI, which will be the Competent Authority to administer and operationalise the Act.

sections.label: Citation year change and Sitting suspension
sections.summary: The citation year will change from 2023 to 2024, Mr Leong's dissent will be recorded, and the Sitting is suspended until 3.40 pm.

sentences.speaker: The Chairman
sentences.text: The citation year "2023" will be changed to "2024", as indicated in the Order Paper Supplement.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: Mr Leong, we will have your dissent recorded.

sentences.speaker: Mr Speaker
sentences.text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.40 pm.
